title: Radicals & Complex Numbers
summary: Radicals simplify by pulling out perfect-power factors; you add like radicals, multiply with the product rule, and rationalize denominators. When a square root of a negative appears, complex numbers with $i=\sqrt{-1}$ extend the number system.

radical.in_class: Index shows which root; simplify by extracting perfect powers.

radicand.in_class: Factor it to find perfect-power pieces.

rationalize.plain: Clear a radical from a denominator.
rationalize.in_class: Multiply by a form of 1 (the radical or a conjugate).

complex number.plain: A number $a+bi$ with real and imaginary parts.

like radicals.plain: Radicals with the same index and radicand.

product rule (radicals).in_class: Splits a radicand to extract perfect squares.

concept_sections.heading: Simplifying radicals
concept_sections.explanation: Factor the radicand and pull out perfect-power factors: $\sqrt{50}=\sqrt{25\cdot2}=5\sqrt2$. For higher roots, extract groups matching the index.
math_steps: Factor out the largest perfect power.

concept_sections.heading: Operating on radicals
concept_sections.explanation: Add or subtract only like radicals (same index and radicand). Multiply with $\sqrt a\,\sqrt b=\sqrt{ab}$, then simplify.
math_steps: Add/subtract like radicals by their coefficients.

concept_sections.heading: Rationalizing denominators
concept_sections.explanation: Remove a radical from the bottom by multiplying by it (single term) or by the conjugate (a sum/difference), which uses the difference-of-squares to clear the root.
math_steps: Single radical: multiply top and bottom by that radical.

concept_sections.heading: The imaginary unit
concept_sections.explanation: Define $i=\sqrt{-1}$, so $i^2=-1$. Then $\sqrt{-9}=3i$, and higher powers cycle $i,-1,-i,1$.

concept_sections.heading: Complex arithmetic
concept_sections.explanation: Add/subtract real and imaginary parts separately; multiply with FOIL using $i^2=-1$; divide by multiplying by the complex conjugate.
math_steps: Add: combine real with real, imaginary with imaginary.

real_world_examples.title: Diagonal of a screen
real_world_examples.scenario: A TV's diagonal from width and height.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The Pythagorean theorem gives a radical like $\sqrt{w^2+h^2}$ to simplify.

real_world_examples.title: AC circuit impedance
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Impedance is a complex number $R+iX$; its magnitude uses $\sqrt{R^2+X^2}$.

real_world_examples.title: Signal phase
real_world_examples.scenario: Waves described by real and imaginary parts.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Complex numbers encode amplitude and phase compactly.
